newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists' call for talks rejected.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists' call for talks rejected.

text.p: A fresh offer by Bulgaria's ruling Socialists for talks on a coalition government was rejected on Sunday and the party now looks set to form an all-Socialist cabinet despite widespread opposition.

Both the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) and President Petar Stoyanov quickly slammed the door on talks unless the Socialists first gave back the mandate they received last week to form a new cabinet.

A UDF spokeswoman said discussions could take place only after the Socialists returned their mandate. A presidential spokesman said the president could not broker talks between political parties while the Socialists still held the mandate.

In proposing coalition talks on Sunday, Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov said that if his offer were turned down then the Socialists would announce their new cabinet on Monday afternoon. It would be voted in parliament on Tuesday.
During a six-hour meeting of Socialist leaders on Sunday, student protesters surrounded the party headquarters chanting anti-communist slogans.
They brandished effigies of Parvanov and Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the party's nominee for premier.
Opposition and student protesters demanding an immediate general election staged a 28th day of strikes, rallies and blockades around the country.
Bulgaria's government has been paralysed since December when Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned.

While the Balkan state has sunk further into political and economic crisis, urgent legislation has been left unattended such as voting the 1997 budget, and adopting measures to support the lev and other steps to tackle the economic crisis.
Both the European Union and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have said that there could be no efforts to help Bulgaria out of crisis until a stable government was in place.
The UDF and student demonstrators have vowed to intensify their nationwide protests if the Socialists vote a new cabinet through parliament.

Edging towards economic collapse, Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate with foreign lenders and set up a tough fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.
The Socialists have an absolute majority in parliament and, barring defections, seem confident of passing their cabinet.
But many people fear a repeat of the violence which broke out between police and demonstrators who besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10.
Dobrev tried on Friday to propose a compromise way out but failed to win the backing of the party leadership.

UDF leader Ivan Kostov, demanding nothing short of quick elections, told the daily rally in Sofia that the Socialists have "two choices, either to go in peace or to go in war, and we are prepared for both".
At Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia, several hundred opposition supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fifth day.
Protesters warmed themselves at wood fires on barricades and said that if the Socialists formed a new cabinet they would set up their barricades outside parliament.
Miners and steelworkers went on strike, and protesters blocked main roads around the second city of Plovdiv and the highway to the border with the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.
State radio said distribution staff at the Neftohim refinery were operating only a minimum service, supplying schools, hospitals and the police.
In Sofia, students blocked road junctions and calmly set up chessboards or played cards on tram lines.
